questions.question: A batch contains portrait receipts and landscape charts at native resolution. What does patch-n'-pack do before transformer attention?
options: Patch each image at its native size and concatenate variable-length patch sequences.
Resize every image to one square and pad all sequences to the same length.
Crop every image to its center square and discard the remaining pixels.
Encode each image separately and average all image embeddings.
questions.explanation: Patch-n’-pack converts each image at its native resolution into its own patch sequence, concatenates those variable-length sequences, and uses a block-diagonal mask to keep images separate. Square resizing distorts aspect ratio; padding wastes attention on empty tokens.

questions.question: Two packed images have patch-sequence lengths 4 and 9. What packed length and block-diagonal mask nonzero count result?
options: 18 tokens and 162 allowed cells, from padding two length-9 images.
9 tokens and 81 allowed cells, from keeping only the longer image.
13 tokens and 97 allowed cells, from 4+9 and 4^2+9^2.
13 tokens and 169 allowed cells, from a full 13x13 mask.
questions.explanation: The packed length is 4+9=13. Only within-image pairs are allowed, so the mask contains 4²+9²=16+81=97 ones; padding both to 9 would create two 9×9 blocks instead. Cross-image entries remain masked.

questions.question: What position information does Qwen2-VL's M-RoPE attach to each visual patch?
options: A separate text-token position from the user prompt.
A class label and the patch's RGB channel count.
Temporal, row, and column coordinates for the patch.
Only one learned absolute index in a fixed square grid.
questions.explanation: M-RoPE assigns each patch temporal, row, and column coordinates, then uses those axes in rotary position encoding. A single fixed learned grid index does not represent arbitrary spatial and temporal dimensions.

questions.question: A frozen vision encoder accepts only 336x336 crops, but the image contains small chart labels. Which high-resolution strategy fits the lesson?
options: Native M-RoPE without changing the frozen encoder's supported input size.
Drop half the patches before creating any crop or thumbnail.
Square-resize to one crop and expect the labels to remain equally detailed.
AnyRes tiling with a global thumbnail, encoding each crop at the supported size.
questions.explanation: AnyRes preserves detail for a fixed-size encoder by splitting the image into supported 336×336 crops and adding a resized global thumbnail. M-RoPE changes positional encoding but cannot make a frozen encoder accept an unsupported image size.

questions.question: A mixed batch has image patch lengths 256, 576, 729, and 1024. What packed sequence length and allowed mask-cell count should it have?
options: 1,024 tokens and 1,048,576 allowed cells, from keeping only the largest image.
2,585 tokens and 2,585 allowed cells.
2,585 tokens and 6,682,225 allowed cells.
2,585 tokens and 1,977,329 allowed cells.
questions.explanation: Packed length is 256+576+729+1024=2,585. Allowed cells are the four within-image squares: 65,536+331,776+531,441+1,048,576=1,977,329; each image contributes its own n_i² block, while cross-image cells stay masked. A dense 2,585² mask would mix images.

questions.question: A product needs variable aspect ratios with a selectable 256-, 729-, or 1024-token budget from one checkpoint. Which approach matches the lesson?
options: M-RoPE, which requires one exact fixed token budget for every image.
Square-resize, which preserves every native-resolution patch.
LLaVA-NeXT AnyRes, which always uses a single fixed 336 crop.
SigLIP 2 NaFlex, which serves several token budgets without retraining.
questions.explanation: NaFlex lets one SigLIP 2 checkpoint serve multiple sequence lengths, including selectable 256, 729, or 1024-token budgets. AnyRes tiles an image for a fixed encoder and adds a thumbnail rather than selecting a native-flex budget.
